props.title: Parasite
props.initialSlug: Parasitic creatures turn victims into ravenous zombies

sections.content: You're likely thinking of the wrong **Parasite (1982)**! The groundbreaking 2019 Oscar winner from Bong Joon-ho overshadows this 1982 B-movie creature feature. The '82 **Parasite** was one of the many attempts to cash in on the 3D movie craze of the early 1980s, following hits like **Friday the 13th Part III** (1982). Produced by Charles Band, who would later become famous for the **Puppet Master** series (1989), this sci-fi horror follows a scientist creating parasitic creatures that turn victims into zombies.

sections.content: The 1982 **Parasite** belongs to a specific breed of early '80s horror that experimented with 3D technology. Films like **Jaws 3-D** (1983) and **Amityville 3-D** (1983) tried capitalizing on the gimmick, usually with diminishing returns. While the '82 film is mostly forgotten, it marks an interesting transition period between the practical effects-driven horror of the 1970s and the more effects-heavy films that would dominate later in the decade.

For superior parasitic horror from this era, look to David Cronenberg's early works. Shivers (1975) and **Rabid** (1977) explore similar themes of infection and bodily invasion with much more artistic and philosophical weight. These films influenced later parasite-themed horror like Slither (2006) and The Faculty (1998), which balanced horror and dark humor. SUBHEAD: Evolution of Parasite Horror

sections.content: The subgenre evolved significantly through the decades. **The Thing** (1982) perfected the paranoid body horror angle, while later films like **Upstream Color** (2013) took more experimental approaches. The massive success of **Parasite** (2019) proved that parasitic themes could transcend pure horror to deliver cutting social commentary. Even video game adaptations like **The Last of Us** (2023) series draw from this rich tradition of parasitic horror.
